idiom_name: Pekko/Akka pool router with N routees (in-JVM)
implementation_notes: The JVM actor default: a pool router (RoundRobinPool or BalancingPool) owns N routees and forwards each message to exactly one of them, which is the competing-consumer contract with supervision and lifecycle built in; BalancingPool shares one mailbox (work stealing) while RoundRobinPool gives every routee its own mailbox and rotates sends. What replaces a hand-written dispatcher is the router actor; what remains the application's job is acknowledgement, retry and backpressure policy.
pitfalls: Default supervision restarts a failed routee but the in-flight message is gone: at-most-once, so durable work needs explicit acknowledgement/retry or a broker.
RoundRobinPool is blind to load - a slow routee keeps getting its share; BalancingPool (shared mailbox) routes by mailbox pressure instead.
Mailboxes are unbounded by default: without a bounded mailbox or ack-based flow control, a slow pool grows memory instead of backpressuring the producer.

variants.name: Kafka consumer group (broker-level competition)
variants.implementation_notes: Cross-process Scala deployments usually express the pattern through a broker: each member of a Kafka consumer group owns a disjoint subset of partitions, so partitions behave as point-to-point channels and the group coordinator - not an actor router - decides which consumer gets which work; Pekko Connectors Kafka wraps this in a Stream[s] pipeline with committed offsets. It is the durability and elasticity story the actor router cannot provide, at the cost of ordering only within a partition and of rebalances that pause processing.
variants.code_sketch:
val consumerSettings = ConsumerSettings(system, new StringDeserializer, new StringDeserializer)
  .withGroupId("orders")
  .withProperty(ConsumerConfig.AUTO_OFFSET_RESET_CONFIG, "earliest")

Consumer
  .plainSource(consumerSettings, Subscriptions.topics("orders"))
  .mapAsync(parallelism = n)(msg => process(msg).map(_ => msg))
  .runWith(Sink.ignore)          // group members compete per partition
pitfalls: More group members than partitions leaves members idle; parallelism must respect the partition count.
Offsets committed before the side effect completes turn a crash into message loss; commit after processing (at-least-once).
Rebalances revoke partitions mid-stream: downstream state keyed to a partition must be flushable.
